content.title: Bill Murray’s son Luke lands major sports job as head basketball coach
content.text: Austin Reaves' former teacher explains why he refused to make a backup plan originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay AreaAustin Reaves never made a backup plan.Of all the lessons he learned from Prisscilla Callahan, his former teacher in Arkansas who became like a second mother, that would not be one of them.AdvertisementHis mind, like his career path, was already made up.“He didn’t say, ‘I want to play in the NBA,’” Callahan recalled. “He said, ‘I’m going to play in the NBA.’”Prisscilla Callahan stands on the Cedar Ridge High School basketball court, named after Austin and Spencer Reaves, in Newark, Arkansas. (NBC)Callahan taught career classes at Cedar Ridge High School in Arkansas, where Reaves was a star basketball player who led the team to back-to-back state championships. Students in her class would learn how to fill out applications, make resumés and discuss career options.Skills that Reaves believed he would never need. His application would be the NBA draft, his resume would be his statistics and his career would be as a basketball player.Advertisement“’‘Okay, let’s have a backup plan, just in case,’” Callahan said she told him. “He did not like that at all.”Reaves’ backup plan was to leave no other option. He made sure everything went according to plan, becoming an All-Star caliber player for the Los Angeles Lakers.And when asked to name someone from his hometown outside of his family that helped him get where he is today, he said Mrs. Callahan.“I just want to say thank you from the bottom of my heart,” Reaves said when he and Callahan had a surprise reunion on NBC’s “Launching Legends.” “Keeping me on the right path in school, I know it wasn’t the easiest thing in the world to do. I always told you that this is what I wanted to do, and you kept telling me I needed a backup plan. I probably didn’t listen that well.”Dec 19, 2017; Wichita, KS, USA; Wichita State Shockers guard Austin Reaves (12) dribbles the ball up court against Arkansas State Red Wolves guard Rashad Lindsey (1) during the first half at Charles Koch Arena. Mandatory Credit: Peter G. Aiken-USA TODAY Sports‘I was like their school mom’Go to mom.AdvertisementThat’s what Reaves and his older brother, Spencer, would say whenever they needed something, or someone, while at school. They, of course, had a loving and supportive mother at home. But on school grounds, when in need of advice, or a snack, or someone to pin their boutonniere, they went to Mrs. Callahan. “They started calling me ‘mom,’” she said. “I was like their school mom. If they needed anything, ‘Go to mom.’”Reaves first got to know Callahan when she taught Spencer, who was two years older than him, and he would stop in her classroom for a granola bar or to refill his water bottle before basketball practice.She joked that he would eat just about anything, despite his skinny — and tall — frame.Advertisement“Very what I would say lanky in Arkansas terms,” she said. “Buzz haircut. He wasn’t what you would perceive as the basketball star of a small high school or what the movies portray.”He may not have fit the role, but he played it well.Callahan, as yearbook advisor, would attend basketball games to take photographs, getting a front row seat to Reaves’ success on the court.Prisscilla Callahan points to a signed yearbook photo of Austin Reaves at Cedar Ridge High School in Newark, Arkansas. (NBC)It didn’t always translate to the classroom. When Reaves was in Callahan’s class in the computer lab during his senior year, he’d sit at the end computer, where the view between student and teacher was somewhat obstructed. “Didn’t matter if he could see or not,” Callahan said during a tour of her classroom. “Probably watching game film.”AdvertisementFor Reaves, computer lessons didn’t quite resonate the way life lessons did.“Mrs. Callahan was probably one of the biggest influences as a teacher,” he said. “As a student, I wasn’t the greatest student in the world. But she did her best to keep me on path and make me see the bigger picture.”Being a good student can be challenging, but being a good person should be easy.“Her biggest thing throughout the whole thing was be a good person,” he said. “And that stuck with me because when you can do all these good things at the end of the day — sports, whatever — and if people don’t like you for you, then it’s kind of not worth it.”AdvertisementReaves aced that lesson, Callahan said, and he showed it then and now.After practice, Reaves would pass the special education classroom, where one of the kids would wait by the door each day to give him a high-five.“Every day, Austin would come by and stop, give this kid a high-five, he would talk to him,” Callahan said. “Not many 16- and 17-year-olds are going to do that. But it made this boy’s day, every day. He knew Austin was going to come and give him a high-five.”She sees that same warmth in Reaves now when he’s interacting with fans, including the time he met her father, a Vietnam veteran.Advertisement“This is what matters,” she said. “You can score all the points, all the records. But this is what’s important. The way he treats people.”Prisscilla Callahan and Austin Reaves smile next to the Los Angeles Lakers court at Crypto Arena. (Courtesy of Prisscilla Callahan)‘Austin’s going to the Lakers’Callahan watched the 2021 NBA Draft with her husband and daughter, patiently waiting to hear Reaves’ name called.Reaves, who played two years at Wichita State before transferring to Oklahoma, was projected to be a potential second-round pick.His name was never called.“We sit there and we sit there and we sit there and nothing,” Callahan said. “Nothing for hours. And so, by the time it was over, I was just upset and in tears and worried about him because he looked forward to this for so long, and it didn’t happen.”AdvertisementCallahan couldn’t bring herself to reach out to Reaves, so she instead sent a text message to his brother Spencer. He assured her not to worry, something was in the works.Days later while in class, one of Callahan’s students made an announcement.“‘Oh my gosh, Austin’s going to the Lakers,’” she recalled the student saying.Reaves signed a two-way contract, offering the opportunity to split time with the Lakers and the organization’s developmental team.Callahan sent Reaves a text, and her phone soon rang.“He said, ‘I told you so, Mrs. Callahan. I told you,’” Callahan said. “I started crying. I was I was so happy for him.”AdvertisementCallahan got to attend her first Lakers game after NBC arranged for her surprise reunion with Reaves in Los Angeles.“I get to watch you play in person tomorrow night,” she told him.“Oh, you’re coming? Let’s go! Let’s go!” Reaves replied. “It’s been a while.”Now in his fifth season with the Lakers, Reaves averaged a career-best 23.3 points per game while playing alongside LeBron James and Luka Doncic.He’s a star living in Hollywood, set for a lucrative contract extension, making another of his predictions become a reality.“In high school, we did a little simulation where they had to pay bills, and he hated it,” Callahan said. “He said, ‘I’m going to be making enough money where somebody else is going to be paying my bills.’ So, I guess that’s true.”Prisscilla Callahan poses with her daughter, Clancy, and Austin Reaves after a surprise reunion in El Segundo, California. (NBC)‘We consider you family’Still, Reaves hasn’t forgotten where he came from. He returns to his roots, hosting basketball camps in Arkansas with his brother. And Callahan serves as “camp mom,” assisting with whatever is asked of her.Advertisement“The kids at camp will ask me, ‘Are you Spencer and Austin’s mom?’ And I’m like, ‘No, I’m 4-foot-11. I’m not their mom. She’s a lot taller than I am. I’m a school mom.’”But also far more than that.“We consider you family,” Reaves said.Callahan feels the same, saying she thinks of Austin and Spencer as sons — and her daughter Clancy considers them older brothers.“He said it, family,” Callahan said. “Their parents did an amazing job raising them. And I’ve told them before, if I had a son or sons, I would want them to be just like them.”But maybe with a backup plan, just in case.“Now [Austin] has the business on the side with the shoes and everything,” she said. “So, he is using that, I guess, as a backup plan.”
